chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umeyr, from Abu Ayoub, who said:

Muhammad ibn Muslim asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) and I was listening: 'Regarding the traveler who considers staying for ten days,' he said: 'Let him complete the prayer. And if he does not know whether he will stay a day or more, let him count thirty days, then let him complete [the prayer]. And if he stayed a day or one prayer [time],' Muhammad ibn Muslim said to him: 'It has reached me that you said five [days].' He said: 'I had said that.' Abu Ayoub said: 'So I said, 'May I be sacrificed for you, can it be less than five?' He said: 'No.'

key_terms.فِدَاكَ: May I be your ransom (a term of respect)

ai.seo_question: How many days must a traveler stay to be considered a resident and pray full prayers instead of shortening them?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi clarifies the jurisprudential threshold for distinguishing between a traveler (Musafir) and a resident (Muqim) by establishing ten days as the standard for full prayer and thirty days as the default for uncertainty. It specifically addresses the scholarly debate regarding the minimum duration for shortening prayers, with Imam al-Sadiq (AS) confirming that stays shorter than five days do not qualify for Qasr, thereby refining the application of the 'ten-day rule' in Shia fiqh. The narration highlights the importance of precise intention (niyyah) and the practical implications of varying scholarly opinions on the lower bound of travel duration.
